fig18_1: Two side-by-side line plots over the interval from minus one to one at N equals sixteen. The left panel shows the third eigenmode, where open circles for the numerical solution sit exactly on the smooth exact curve cosine of three pi x over two, agreeing to eight decimals, with the eigenvalue near twenty-two point two zero six six one matching three pi over two squared. The right panel shows the fifteenth eigenmode, which also looks smooth but bunches its oscillations near the two endpoints rather than spreading evenly like the exact sine of fifteen pi x over two; its eigenvalue near three thousand one hundred seventy-four point seven nine is wrong, too large by a factor of about five point seven compared with the exact value near five hundred fifty-five point one seven, illustrating that visual smoothness alone does not guarantee a correct eigenfunction.
fig18_2: Two panels comparing two formulations of the same eigenproblem. The left panel plots absolute error against mode number on a logarithmic vertical axis, with blue circles for the boundary-bordered pencil and coral squares for the basis-recombined regular problem lying on top of each other, while teal crosses showing their difference sit far below at roughly one point seven times ten to the power minus twelve, machine noise, confirming both methods deliver the same spectrum. The right panel is a heatmap of the base-ten logarithm of the absolute matrix entries of the bordered pencil, revealing two thin identity-like boundary rows across the very top and very bottom.
fig18_3: A semi-logarithmic plot of absolute eigenvalue error against mode number for three resolutions, N equals sixteen, thirty-two, and sixty-four. A dashed horizontal line marks the good tolerance of ten to the power minus two, and dotted vertical lines at N over two mark the heuristic cliff. Each curve stays low and geometrically accurate across the resolved modes, then turns sharply upward at the cliff into the unresolved range, where error rises to the order of the eigenvalue itself; the number of good modes is six at N equals sixteen, fifteen at N equals thirty-two, and thirty-four at N equals sixty-four.
fig18_4: Three panels illustrating the rational Chebyshev TB n map and basis. The left panel plots the algebraic map x equals ell t over the square root of one minus t squared for four values of the scale parameter ell, with vertical dotted asymptotes at t equals plus and minus one carrying x to plus and minus infinity, and larger ell stretching the interior of the curve further outward. The middle panel shows collocation grids at N equals twenty-four as rows of horizontal tick marks laid over a Gaussian-like target profile, where small ell equals one keeps nodes tightly clustered near x equals zero while ell equals eight scatters nodes far out into the tails. The right panel plots the first five basis functions, TB zero through TB four, at ell equals two, each leveling off toward a constant as the magnitude of x grows toward infinity.
fig18_5: Two panels showing the cost of working on an infinite interval for the harmonic oscillator. The left panel plots absolute eigenvalue error against mode number on a logarithmic vertical scale at N equals sixteen and thirty-two with scale parameter ell equals four; the cliff arrives earlier than for the bounded Laplacian, giving only four trusted modes at N equals sixteen versus six, and ten at N equals thirty-two versus fifteen. The right panel is a scan over ell at fixed N equals thirty-two, where ell equals four yields the most trusted modes at ten, ell equals two crowds nodes near the origin and gives only seven, and ell equals eight wastes nodes in the tails and gives only five.
tbl18_1: A regression-test table listing the scaled ordinal drifts of the eight suspect modes from j equals thirteen through twenty, each compared against the closed-form prediction j over four.
fig18_6: Two panels applying the drift diagnostic, on the left to the Dirichlet Laplacian and on the right to the harmonic oscillator, each comparing resolutions N one equals thirty-two and N two equals forty-eight. In both, blue circles show the reciprocal of the ordinal drift and coral crosses the reciprocal of the nearest-neighbour drift, plotted against mode number, with a sharp cliff dropping from high reliable values down to noisy small ones that separates trusted from suspect modes. The Laplacian shows sixteen trusted modes near N one over two, while the oscillator shows only nine because of the infinite-interval tax, and the two diagnostics agree on where the cliff falls.
fig18_7: Two panels for the Poschl-Teller potential with nu equals four. The left panel plots the lowest twenty-five eigenvalues at N one equals sixty as circles and N two equals ninety-six as crosses against index; the four exact bound-state energies at minus sixteen, minus nine, minus four, and minus one, marked by horizontal teal dashes, are hit to machine precision so the two symbols coincide, while the continuum modes above energy zero drift apart between the two resolutions. The right panel shows the reciprocal drift diagnostic against mode number, with a cliff at mode five that separates the four bound states plus the marginal zero-energy mode from the under-resolved continuum above.
fig18_8: Three panels showing how a naive formulation manufactures a fake instability. The left panel plots the finite spectrum on a real axis at N equals thirty-two as circles and N equals forty-eight as crosses, each showing exactly one isolated large positive eigenvalue far from the rest. The middle panel is a log-log plot of that single spurious positive eigenvalue against resolution from N equals sixteen to two hundred fifty-six, rising along a power law that approaches the order N to the fourth asymptote from below, with empirical slope climbing from about three point four to about three point six. The right panel confirms that the cured formulation has zero positive eigenvalues at every resolution.
fig18_9: Two panels performing condition-number surgery on the fourth-order clamped eigenproblem. The left panel plots condition number against resolution N on log-log axes, with blue circles for the naive fourth-derivative bordered pencil and coral squares for the Heinrichs basis built from one minus x squared all squared times Chebyshev polynomials; both grow steeply but the Heinrichs curve sits about eight times lower, and dashed reference lines of slope N to the eighth and N to the fourth frame them as asymptotes. The right panel plots the error in the first eigenvalue for the two discretisations, where Heinrichs is strictly more accurate at small N while both flatten onto a common conditioning floor at large N.
fig18_10: Three panels demonstrating one-mode-at-a-time iterative solvers, each plotting the iterate value against iteration count. The left panel shows the power method climbing and converging to the largest eigenvalue near forty-nine thousand nine hundred thirty-nine. The middle panel shows inverse iteration with three shifts, mu equals five, ninety, and two hundred fifty, each rapidly locking onto an interior eigenvalue near two point four seven, eighty-eight point eight three, and two hundred forty-six point seven four within at most twenty iterations. The right panel is a cautionary case where a shift mu near fifty point five eight placed exactly between two adjacent eigenvalues near thirty-nine point four eight and sixty-one point six eight fails to settle on either and converges only slowly.
fig18_11: Two panels on safely tracking a parameter-dependent spectrum. The left panel shows the leading eigenvalue lambda one as a function of alpha and beta, computed by full QR at every node of a nine-by-nine coarse grid marked with white dots, with contour lines drawn through the resulting eigenvalue surface. The right panel is a fine scan over beta at alpha equals zero, where the safe blue curve re-runs QR at every beta and smoothly tracks lambda one rising from about two point four seven to about three point four four, while the naive coral curve, continuing inverse iteration from a bad shift, accidentally jumps to and follows lambda two and ends near twelve point zero six instead of three point four four.
fig18_12: Two panels showing a detour into the complex plane around a singularity at y equals zero. The left panel plots three parabolic integration contours y of x equals x plus i Delta times x squared minus one for Delta equal to zero point two five, zero point five zero, and zero point seven five, each arcing below the real axis to connect y equals minus one to y equals plus one while skirting the pole at y equals zero marked by a purple cross. The right panel plots the first seven eigenvalues sorted by magnitude at N equals forty for the three Delta values in the complex plane; all are complex, and the three traces overlap for the lowest converged modes but fan apart for the higher under-resolved modes.
tbl18_2: A table listing the first four eigenvalues at N equals forty and Delta equals zero point five from the complex-plane detour, computed independently in Python, MATLAB, and Julia and shown to agree.
